bearings.paper_claim: The paper's 'most reliable path' maximizes on-time arrival probability Phi((b - mean)/SD) for a travel-time budget b. It states that this objective 'is non-additive and cannot be solved by existing' shortest-path methods, so it uses M-B dominance plus multi-criteria label-setting (MRP-TS) rather than Dijkstra.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 2, p. 6 (non-additivity, text line ~489); Sec. 3, pp. 7-13 (MRP-TS; Prop. 4 for MRP-RS, Prop. 5 for MRP-RA)
bearings.system_side: The recruitment chain is a max-product path: distToTarget runs a Dijkstra-style max-product search and tracePath follows the argmax of PE*dT. Reliability is the product of per-hop kernel probabilities, and chainHold is the product of activeP(p) with ASKM 0.07. The code comment cites Chen, Shi, Zhang & Lam 2016 as grounding for 'maximize the probability the whole chain holds' and calls the result 'PROVABLY-OPTIMAL'. A product of independent edge probabilities is additive in -log p (the Frank / Bellman reliable-path case), so Dijkstra is the right tool. That object is not the one this paper solves.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper supports the system's method only in name. Its deadline-reliability algorithm would carry over only if the system modeled a stochastic time-to-join per hop and asked for P(target joins before a deadline such as markup), which it does not. As built, the right grounding is the classical max-product or -log p shortest path, not this paper. Road data, 2009 Wuhan; no legislative content.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper: "the most reliable path problem is non-additive and cannot be solved by existing deterministic shortest path algorithms (e.g., Dijkstra's algorithm)" confirmed; Props. 4 and 5 exist in Sec. 3. Code: tpl:734 distToTarget is max-product Dijkstra; tpl:735-739 comment says PROVABLY-OPTIMAL and cites Chen, Shi, Zhang & Lam, Transportmetrica B 2016; ASKM=0.07, activeP, chainHold at 748-751. Page for non-additivity corrected 7 -> 6. Page numbers follow the page-number lines in the extracted text (approximate).

bearings.paper_claim: The method assumes independent link travel times. Sec. 2 notes the assumption can be relaxed with a two-level hierarchical network model (Chen et al. 2012); the Conclusions list correlation first among future directions, saying it is omitted "for simplicity" although urban link times are strongly correlated. Normal approximation of path travel time, checked against Monte Carlo ground truth on 100 randomly selected Wuhan paths, averages 98.3% accuracy at the 10th percentile and 94.9% at the 90th.
bearings.paper_location: Sec. 2, p. 5 (independence + hierarchical relaxation, line ~282); Sec. 4.1, Fig. 2, p. 15; Sec. 5, p. 19-20 (for simplicity)
bearings.system_side: chainHold multiplies per-hop activeP values as if every ask succeeds or fails independently, and the comment calls it a 'conservative floor' (rerouting only improves it). The asks in one chain share the same bill, issue salience, party context and ASKM lever, so their outcomes are likely positively correlated. Under positive correlation the product is not a floor on joint success. Paths are also ranked by passive pathReliability, while chainHold, which is shown to the user, is computed on the active-ask scale.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Only the structural point transfers: path reliability built as a product or sum of independent per-link terms inherits an independence assumption that the source paper itself flags as its main limitation. The direction and size of correlation among legislator asks is untested. The UI already labels the figure as scenario output, not an empirical probability (tpl:1119, 1155).
bearings.verifier_note: Numbers 98.3% / 94.9% / 100 paths confirmed. Location "Sec. 1, p. 5" was wrong: the independence assumption sits in Sec. 2 (Problem statement), not the Introduction. Code side confirmed: chainHold multiplies activeP per hop and the comment calls it a conservative floor (tpl:751); tracePath ranks by passive PE while chainHold uses activeP; tooltips at tpl:1119 and 1155 say scenario output, not empirical probability. The claim that legislator asks are positively correlated is the analyst's reasoning, untested. Page numbers follow the page-number lines in the extracted text (approximate).

bearings.paper_claim: MRP-TS's optimality is proven (Props. 4-5, Lemmas 1-3) and also checked empirically: it returns the same optimal paths as an independent multi-criteria A* on the same budgets, across 100 O-D pairs.
bearings.system_side: The chain is labelled 'PROVABLY-OPTIMAL', but no second algorithm reproduces it. Agent reading (UNVERIFIED, DE-062): distToTarget(t) propagates d[v] = d[u]*PE[u][v] outward from the target, which is the reliability of target -> v. tracePath then walks sponsor -> target scoring PE[cur][v]*dT[v]. PE is asymmetric because of the receiver edge_mult EMU[v] and the source_shock/target_resistance role priors, so dT is computed in the reverse direction from the one tracePath needs. Also, dT ignores the 'dropped' set while tracePath skips dropped nodes, so the greedy walk can stall (reached=false) even when a path that avoids them exists.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Chen et al.'s validation design (exact algorithm vs an independent exact solver on the same inputs) transfers directly, since it is a software check, not an empirical claim. The direction mismatch matters only when PE is asymmetric. That happens when the bundle carries emult or the issue's role priors are non-unit; with neutral multipliers the walk is exact. The size of the effect is bounded by the EMU range [0.80, 1.20] and has not been measured.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper: averages over 100 random O-D pairs; with budgets from the multi-criteria A* alpha-reliable solver, MRP-TS "can determine the same optimal paths as the multi-criteria A* algorithm". Code re-read independently: distToTarget(t) sets d[t]=1 and relaxes d[v]=d[u]*PE[u][v] (reliability t->v); tracePath scores PE[cur][v]*dT[v] going sponsor->target; dT ignores dropped while tracePath skips dropped (tpl:734,740). ADJ is symmetrised (tpl:547), so asymmetry comes only from EMU[v] (tpl:586), and from source_shock/target_resistance role priors (tpl:595-597); edge_mult range [0.80,1.20] confirmed at fec/members/receptivity_layer.py:47. This verifier reproduced the code reading by a second read, but no executed comparison against an exact solver exists, so the finding stays UNVERIFIED in the DE-062 sense until run. Page numbers follow the page-number lines in the extracted text (approximate).

bearings.paper_claim: Mean-Budget dominance with multi-criteria label-setting finds exact non-dominated path sets fast. 11,087-18,115 non-dominated paths are handled in 162-276 ms on Wuhan. The FSD label-correcting benchmark generates 225,878 paths, of which 95.09% are M-B dominated.
bearings.system_side: The cosponsor route Pareto front is assembled from five scalarized greedy runs (lambda in {0, 0.5, 1, 2, 4}, value = (gain - lambda(1-p))/cost), then filtered for dominance. It is an approximate front over the points those runs visit, not an exact non-dominated set. Points in non-convex regions of the front cannot be reached by any lambda.
bearings.transfer_conditions: This is a weak, conceptual transfer. Chen's dominance rule is specific to normal path times and a path objective. The cosponsor router grows a recruitment tree with a recruiter capacity cap K, so exact label-setting would need a different dominance relation. It is relevant only if Paul wants the front to be exact rather than illustrative.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper: 275.69 ms (alpha 0.1) and 162.47 ms (alpha 0.4); 18,115 and 11,087 non-dominated paths; BSP-LC generated 225,878 FSD non-dominated paths, 95.09% M-B dominated (vs MRP-TS at alpha 0.1). Code: cosponsor_route.py build_route uses val=(gain-lam*(1-p))/c in a greedy heap with out-degree cap K; lam in (0,0.5,1,2,4); front filtered by dominated() at lines ~40-76. Confirmed. Page numbers follow the page-number lines in the extracted text (approximate).

bearings.paper_claim: Penalizing path variability through SD makes the path objective non-additive, so Dijkstra loses exactness. Exact solutions need multi-criteria labels such as mean and variance.
bearings.system_side: The staffer router adds uncertainty linearly per hop: cost = -ln(0.8 x strength) + w x u, with u explicitly 'not a probability'. Because the penalty is a per-hop sum, bidirectional Dijkstra with heuristic 0 stays exact, and the code backs this with exact-arithmetic tie handling.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The paper serves as a boundary condition, not a criticism. The current additive design is correctly solved. If uncertainty were ever restated as an SD aggregated over the route, or as a probability of a usable introduction by a date, Dijkstra would no longer be exact and Chen-style label-setting would apply. Route costs remain heuristic outputs, never introduction or access probabilities (D-025).
bearings.verifier_note: Paper non-additivity confirmed (Sec. 2). Code: staffer_closeness_routes.py docstring describes bidirectional Dijkstra with heuristic 0 and exact-arithmetic tie pass (lines 12-21); _hop_cost = -log(HOP_FACTOR*strength) + weight*u (115-116); provenance formula says u is not a probability (~999); HOP_FACTOR=.8 at closeness_math.py:20. Confirmed.

related.why: Ahmad's 'strongest path' over social-tie strengths is the classical max-product or -log-weight path that the dashboard chain actually implements. It is a better-fitting grounding for tpl:735-757 than Chen 2016.
Duan et al. speed up additive single-source shortest paths, which is the problem class the -log p chain and the staffer router belong to. Chen's objective is outside that class.

Both prune dominated partial paths with multi-criteria labels to get non-dominated path sets (MOPBD* path-based expansion vs M-B dominance label-setting). Ren also offers a sub-optimal variant that approximates the Pareto front, so it shows both the exact and approximate options relative to the lambda-scalarized front in cosponsor_route.py.

Lawande reviews heuristic pathfinding (A*, D*, HPA*). Chen's MRP-RA needs an admissible lower-bound heuristic for optimality (Prop. 5), which bears on Paul's wish for heuristic-augmented A* in the routers (both use heuristic 0). Lawande's text does not itself discuss admissibility.

It is co-cited with Chen 2016 in the same code comment (tpl:738-739) as the second grounding for the recruitment chain. Sotoudeh supplies the cosponsorship-influence edges and Chen is cited for the path objective.

summary_issues: Summary says the authors name correlation as "the main open limitation"; the paper lists it first among future research directions ("omitted in this study for simplicity"), not explicitly as the main limitation.

Bearing 2 location cited Sec. 1 for the independence assumption; it is in Sec. 2 and Sec. 5. Page numbers in several bearings were one page high relative to the extracted page-number lines (non-additivity p. 6 not 7; A* match p. 16 not 17).
